contentSections: Quick answer

Anodised aluminium cladding is aluminium whose surface has been thickened by an electrochemical process, so the protective oxide layer becomes part of the metal instead of a paint on top. It gives a durable, metallic look in natural, dark and bronze tones. It suits facades where a true metal appearance matters, and it is one of three main finish routes alongside PVDF and powder coat.
Key takeaways

• Anodising grows the oxide layer from the aluminium itself, so it cannot peel like a coating. • Colour range is narrower than PVDF or powder coat. Metaguise lists natural, dark and bronze anodised options. • Large elevations need careful batch control, because anodised tones can vary between lots. • Ask for the finish specification and the written warranty before you choose.
What anodising actually does

Aluminium forms a thin oxide layer on its own. Anodising thickens that layer in a controlled bath, then seals it. The result is hard and part of the metal. Colour comes from the natural metal or from dye or electrolytic colouring, so the finish keeps the look of aluminium, with its subtle grain, which a painted finish hides.
This is why anodised aluminium cladding is often chosen for facades that want to look like metal rather than colour.

Where anodised aluminium cladding suits Indian projects

• Premium commercial entrances and lobbies, where a real metal surface reads as quality. • Fins, louvers and trims, which are seen close up and benefit from a hard surface. • Minimal residential elevations in natural or dark tones. • Shaded or semi-covered areas, where the surface is protected from the worst exposure.
For seafront buildings, any finish needs a coastal specification and regular rinsing. Read our guide to metal facade systems for coastal homes before you decide.
Limits to know before you specify

1. Colour range is narrower. If your design needs a bright or exact RAL colour, PVDF is the better route. 2. Batch variation. Anodised tones can shift between production lots, so buy all panels for one elevation from a single batch and ask how batches are tracked. 3. Repair is harder. A scratched painted panel can be touched up. A damaged anodised surface is harder to blend. 4. Cleaning matters. Avoid harsh acids, alkalis and abrasives that attack the surface. Our facade maintenance guide lists what to use and what to avoid.
What to ask your facade company

• Which anodised tones are available, and can you see a physical sample? • What coating or film thickness do you specify, and to which standard? • How do you control colour between batches? • What is the written warranty, and what does it cover? • Who installs, and how are panels numbered for sequence?

Frequently asked questions

1. What is anodised aluminium cladding?

It is aluminium panels whose surface oxide layer has been thickened and sealed by an electrochemical process, giving a hard, durable finish that is part of the metal.

2. Is anodised aluminium better than powder coated aluminium?

It depends on the need. Anodising gives a true metallic look and a hard surface. Powder coat offers a wider colour and texture range. PVDF is usually preferred for the strongest weather resistance on large facades.

3. What colours does anodised cladding come in?

Metaguise lists natural, dark and bronze anodised options. Wider colours are usually achieved with PVDF or powder coat.

4. Does anodised aluminium fade?

Quality anodising resists fading, but results depend on the colouring method and sealing. Ask for the specification and written warranty.

5. Is anodised aluminium cladding good for coastal India?

It can perform well when specified and maintained for the environment, including regular fresh-water rinsing. Ask the engineer for a coastal specification.

6. Which is the more durable exterior finish for Indian weather?

PVDF has the strongest published weather and UV performance among common architectural coatings, while anodising is a hard, long-lasting option for metal-look surfaces.
